Semiclassical instanton theory for reaction rates at any temperature: How a rigorous real-time derivation solves the crossover temperature problem

††affiliation: Simons Center for Computational Physical Chemistry, New York University, New York, NY 10003, USA††email: joseph.lawrence@nyu.edu††affiliation: Department of Chemistry, New York University, New York, NY 10003, USA

S1 I. Behaviour of the action as t→∞t\to\infty

In order to analyse the t→∞t\to\infty behaviour of the action, S⁡(t)S(t), in Eq. (24) of the main manuscript, we need to relate the time to the action. To do so we follow the approach given in Ref. 1. This involves first relating the energy of the forward/reverse paths, E±E_{\pm}, to the time, t±=±t−i​τ/2t_{\pm}=\pm t-i\tau/2, and then using the fact that the Euclidean action is related to the energy according to

∂S±∂t±=i​E±\frac{\partial S_{\pm}}{\partial t_{\pm}}=iE_{\pm} (S1)

to integrate to give the desired result.

To do so we begin by noting that the time for the forward path is given by

t+=t−i​τ/2=∫xrxp12​(E+−V​(x))​𝑑x.t_{+}=t-i\tau/2=\int_{x_{r}}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(E_{+}-V(x))}}\mathrm{d}x. (S2)

where x=m​qx=\sqrt{m}q is the mass weighted position, and xrx_{r} and xpx_{p} are the mass weighted locations of the dividing surfaces. To simplify notation we define the maximum of V⁡(x)V(x) to be at the origin, V⁡(x)=V‡−12​ω2​x2V(x)=V^{\ddagger}-\frac{1}{2}\omega^{2}x^{2}, and introduce the energy differences Δ​E+=E+−V‡\Delta E_{+}=E_{+}-V^{\ddagger} and Δ​V​(x)=V⁡(x)−V‡\Delta V(x)=V(x)-V^{\ddagger}. Splitting the path into two halves around the maximum we can thus write

t+=∫xr012​(Δ​E+−Δ​V​(x))​𝑑x+∫0xp12​(Δ​E+−Δ​V​(x))​𝑑x.t_{+}=\int_{x_{r}}^{0}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(\Delta E_{+}-\Delta V(x))}}\mathrm{d}x+\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(\Delta E_{+}-\Delta V(x))}}\mathrm{d}x. (S3)

Now we consider the behaviour as |Δ​E+|→0|\Delta E_{+}|\to 0, taking just the second half of the path we can add and subtract the harmonic contribution to give

∫0xp12​(Δ​E+−Δ​V​(x))​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(\Delta E_{+}-\Delta V(x))}}\mathrm{d}x =∫0xp12​Δ​E++ω2​x2​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\Delta E_{+}+\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x (S4)
+∫0xp12​(Δ​E+−Δ​V​(x))−12​Δ​E++ω2​x2dx\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(\Delta E_{+}-\Delta V(x))}}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\Delta E_{+}+\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x

The harmonic part can then be evaluated analytically to give

∫0xp12​Δ​E++ω2​x2​𝑑x=12​ω​ln⁡(1+xp​ω​(xp​ω+2​Δ​E++xp2​ω2)Δ​E+)\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\Delta E_{+}+\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2\omega}\ln(1+ \frac{x_p \omega\left(x_p\omega+ \sqrt{2\Delta E_+ + x_p^2\omega^2}\right)}{\Delta E_+}) (S5)

where it is assumed that xp>0x_{p}>0. which can be simplified in the limit as |Δ​E+|→0|\Delta E_{+}|\to 0 to give

∫0xp12​Δ​E++ω2​x2​𝑑x∼12​ω​ln⁡(2​xp2​ω2Δ​E+).\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\Delta E_{+}+\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x\sim\frac{1}{2\omega}\ln(\frac{2x_p^2\omega^2}{\Delta E_+}). (S6)

As |Δ​E+|→0|\Delta E_{+}|\to 0 it is clear that the remaining contribution to the forward path approaches a constant i.e.

∫0xp12​(Δ​E+−Δ​V​(x))−12​Δ​E++ω2​x2​𝑑x∼∫0xp12​(−Δ​V​(x))−1ω2​x2​𝑑x\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(\Delta E_{+}-\Delta V(x))}}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\Delta E_{+}+\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x\sim\int_{0}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(-\Delta V(x))}}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x (S7)

Performing the same analysis on the integral from xrx_{r} to 00, and combining the results we obtain the following expression for t+t_{+}

t+∼12​ω​ln⁡(2​xp2​ω2Δ​E+)+12​ω​ln⁡(2​xr2​ω2Δ​E+)+∫xrxp12​(−Δ​V​(x))−1ω2​x2​𝑑xt_{+}\sim\frac{1}{2\omega}\ln(\frac{2x_p^2\omega^2}{\Delta E_+})+\frac{1}{2\omega}\ln(\frac{2x_r^2\omega^2}{\Delta E_+})+\int_{x_{r}}^{x_{p}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(-\Delta V(x))}}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x (S8)

as |Δ​E+|→0|\Delta E_{+}|\to 0. This can then be rearranged to give

Δ​E+∼2​ω2​xr2​xp2​exp⁡(−ω​t++ω​∫xrxp12​(−Δ​V​(x))−1ω2​x2​𝑑x)\Delta E_{+}\sim 2\omega^{2}\sqrt{x_{r}^{2}x_{p}^{2}}\exp(-\omega t_+ + \omega\int_{x_r}^{x_p} \sqrt{\frac{1}{2(- \Delta V(x))}} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{\omega^2 x^2}} \mathrm{d}x ) (S9)

as Re(t+)→∞\real(t_{+})\to\infty. Which we can relate back to the unshifted energy as

E+∼V‡+ω​a⁡(xr,xp)2​exp⁡(−ω​t+)E_{+}\sim V^{\ddagger}+\omega\frac{a(x_{r},x_{p})}{2}\exp(-\omega t_+) (S10)

where

a⁡(xr,xp)=4​ω​xr2​xp2​exp⁡(ω​∫xrxp12​(−Δ​V​(x))−1ω2​x2​𝑑x).a(x_{r},x_{p})=4\omega\sqrt{x_{r}^{2}x_{p}^{2}}\exp( \omega\int_{x_r}^{x_p} \sqrt{\frac{1}{2(- \Delta V(x))}} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{\omega^2 x^2}} \mathrm{d}x ). (S11)

We can then also obtain the equivalent expression for t−=−t−i​τ/2t_{-}=-t-i\tau/2 by noting that

t−=−t−i​τ/2=∫xpxr12​(E−−V​(x))​𝑑x.t_{-}=-t-i\tau/2=\int_{x_{p}}^{x_{r}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(E_{-}-V(x))}}\mathrm{d}x. (S12)

Then to evaluate the final result we just need to be careful to note that (because xr<0x_{r}<0)

∫0xr12​Δ​E−+ω2​x2​𝑑x∼−12​ω​ln⁡(2​xr2​ω2Δ​E−)\int_{0}^{x_{r}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\Delta E_{-}+\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x\sim-\frac{1}{2\omega}\ln(\frac{2x_r^2\omega^2}{\Delta E_-}) (S13)

Hence,

t−∼−12​ω​ln⁡(2​xp2​ω2Δ​E−)−12​ω​ln⁡(2​xr2​ω2Δ​E−)+∫xpxr12​(−Δ​V​(x))−1ω2​x2​𝑑x,t_{-}\sim-\frac{1}{2\omega}\ln(\frac{2x_p^2\omega^2}{\Delta E_-})-\frac{1}{2\omega}\ln(\frac{2x_r^2\omega^2}{\Delta E_-})+\int_{x_{p}}^{x_{r}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2(-\Delta V(x))}}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{\omega^{2}x^{2}}}\mathrm{d}x, (S14)

as |Δ​E−|→0|\Delta E_{-}|\to 0. Swapping the limits we see that −t−-t_{-} is related to Δ​E−\Delta E_{-} as t+t_{+} is to Δ​E+\Delta E_{+} and hence

E−∼V‡+ω​a⁡(xr,xp)2​exp⁡(ω​t−)E_{-}\sim V^{\ddagger}+\omega\frac{a(x_{r},x_{p})}{2}\exp(\omega t_-) (S15)

as Re(t−)→−∞\real(t_{-})\to-\infty.

Now we can combine the energies together and integrate to obtain an expression for the action

S⁡(t)=S+​(t+)+S−​(t−)=S∞+i​∫∞tE+​(t′−i​τ/2)−E−​(−t′−i​τ/2)​d​t′.S(t)=S_{+}(t_{+})+S_{-}(t_{-})=S_{\!\infty}+i\int_{\infty}^{t}E_{+}(t^{\prime}-i\tau/2)-E_{-}(-t^{\prime}-i\tau/2)\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}. (S16)

Inserting the asymptotic definitions of E±E_{\pm} gives

S⁡(t)∼S∞+i​ω​a⁡(xr,xp)2​∫∞te−ω​t′+i​τ​ω/2−e−ω​t′−i​τ​ω/2​d​t′.S(t)\sim S_{\!\infty}+i\omega\frac{a(x_{r},x_{p})}{2}\int_{\infty}^{t}e^{-\omega t^{\prime}+i\tau\omega/2}-e^{-\omega t^{\prime}-i\tau\omega/2}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}. (S17)

Finally evaluating the integral and combining together the complex exponentials we obtain

S⁡(t)∼S∞+a⁡(xr,xp)​sin⁡(ω​τ/2)​e−ω​tS(t)\sim S_{\!\infty}+a(x_{r},x_{p})\sin(\omega\tau/2)e^{-\omega t} (S18)

as t→∞t\to\infty.

S2 II. Behaviour of the prefactor as t→∞t\to\infty

The prefactor in Eq. (24) of the main manuscript has the form

A⁡(t)\displaystyle A(t) =−14​m2​C+​C−(2​π​ℏ)2​(∂S−∂sr​∂S+∂sp−∂S−∂sp​∂S−∂sr−∂S+∂sp​∂S+∂sr+∂S−∂sp​∂S+∂sr)\displaystyle=\frac{-1}{4m^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{C_{+}C_{-}}{(2\pi\hbar)^{2}}}\Bigg(\frac{\partial S_{-}}{\partial s_{r}}\frac{\partial S_{+}}{\partial s_{p}}-\frac{\partial S_{-}}{\partial s_{p}}\frac{\partial S_{-}}{\partial s_{r}}-\frac{\partial S_{+}}{\partial s_{p}}\frac{\partial S_{+}}{\partial s_{r}}+\frac{\partial S_{-}}{\partial s_{p}}\frac{\partial S_{+}}{\partial s_{r}}\Bigg) (S19)

where

C±=−∂2S±∂sr​∂sp.C_{\pm}=-\frac{\partial^{2}S_{\pm}}{\partial s_{r}\partial s_{p}}. (S20)

In order to obtain an expression for the prefactor of the correlation function as t→∞t\to\infty we, therefore, need to consider the derivatives of the action with respect to the end points, making use of results from the previous section.

To begin with we note that by defining

Δ​S±\displaystyle\Delta S_{\!\pm} =Δ​S±|t=∞+∫±∞t±i​Δ​E±​(t±′)​d​t±′\displaystyle=\Delta S_{\pm}|_{t=\infty}+\int_{\pm\infty}^{t_{\pm}}i\Delta E_{\pm}(t^{\prime}_{\pm})\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}_{\pm} (S21)
=Δ​S±|t=∞∓i​a​(xr,xp)2​exp⁡(∓ω​t±)\displaystyle=\Delta S_{\pm}|_{t=\infty}\mp\frac{ia(x_{r},x_{p})}{2}\exp(\mp\omega t_{\pm})

S3 III. Behaviour of Upadhyayula and Pollak’s theory as ℏ→0\hbar\to 0

Recently, Upadhyayula and Pollak have suggested a theory that they name “uniform semiclassical instanton rate theory”. Here we clarify that, while their theory is based on the uniform semiclassical transmission probability of Kemble,Kemble (1935) it is not a rigorous uniform semiclassical theory in τ\tau as ℏ→0\hbar\to 0. It is important to stress that Upadhyayula and Pollak do not explicitly claim their theory to be uniform in τ\tau as ℏ→0\hbar\to 0. Nevertheless, for the general reader confusion about this issue may arise, particularly given they derive their result starting from a rigorous uniform semiclassical theory in EE as ℏ→0\hbar\to 0.

Upadhyayula and Pollak’s theory can be written in one dimension as

kRef. 3​Zr=e−Φτ(ℰτ)/ℏ2​π​τ\displaystyle k_{\text{Ref.~\cite[citenum]{\@@bibref{Number}{Upadhyayula2023UniformInstanton}{}{}}}}Z_{r}=\frac{e^{-\Phi_{\tau}(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})/\hbar}}{2\pi\tau} [π​τ2/2​ℏΦτ′′​(ℰτ)​erfc​(−τ2/2​ℏΦτ′′​(ℰτ))+exp⁡(−τ22​ℏ​Φτ′′​(ℰτ))]\displaystyle\left[\sqrt{\frac{\pi\tau^{2}/2\hbar}{\Phi_{\tau}^{\prime\prime}(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})}}\mathrm{erfc}\left(-\sqrt{\frac{\tau^{2}/2\hbar}{\Phi_{\tau}^{\prime\prime}(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})}}\right)\right.+\left.\exp(-\frac{\tau^2}{2\hbar\Phi_\tau''(\mathcal{E}_\tau)})\vphantom{\sqrt{\frac{\tau^{2}/2\hbar}{\Phi_{\tau}^{\prime\prime}(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})}}}\right] (S37)

where the effective action Φτ​(E)\Phi_{\tau}(E) is defined as

Φτ​(E)=τ​E+ℏ​ln⁡(1+eW⁡(E)/ℏ)\Phi_{\tau}(E)=\tau E+\hbar\ln\left(1+e^{W(E)/\hbar}\right) (S38)

and the stationary energy, ℰτ\mathcal{E}_{\tau}, is given by

Φτ′​(ℰτ)=τ+W′​(ℰτ)1+e−W(ℰτ)/ℏ=0.\Phi_{\tau}^{\prime}(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})=\tau+\frac{W^{\prime}(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})}{1+e^{-W(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})/\hbar}}=0. (S39)

Here, W⁡(E)W(E) is the reduced action (the Legendre transform of Sinst​(τ)S_{\!\rm inst}(\tau)). Note that if W⁡(E)W(E) is monotonic and τ⁡(E)\tau(E) is monotonic then it follows that τ\tau is also a monotonic function of ℰτ\mathcal{E}_{\tau}

τ=−W′​(ℰτ)1+e−W(ℰτ)/ℏ.\tau=-\frac{W^{\prime}(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})}{1+e^{-W(\mathcal{E}_{\tau})/\hbar}}. (S40)

To illustrate the asymptotic behaviour of Upadhyayula and Pollak’s theory we consider the asymmetric Eckart barrier (defined in main text) at various values of ℏ\hbar. With the exception of ℏ\hbar, the parameters of the model are defined to be the same in reduced units as those in the main text with m=1m=1, L=8/3​πL=8/\sqrt{3\pi}, V1=(6/π)14V_{1}=(6/\pi)^{\frac{1}{4}}, V2=(24/π)14V_{2}=(24/\pi)^{\frac{1}{4}}, and ℏ\hbar varying from 11 to 1/81/8. Note that varying ℏ\hbar while keeping the other constants fixed simply corresponds to a change in the definition of the reduced units. An asymptotic theory should obey,

limℏ→0kapproxkexact=1,\lim_{\hbar\to 0}\frac{k_{\rm approx}}{k_{\rm exact}}=1, (S41)

and a uniform asymptotic theory should obey this at every value of the uniform parameter (in this case τ\tau). Hence, by plotting kapproxkexact\frac{k_{\rm approx}}{k_{\rm exact}} as a function of τ\tau for successively smaller values of ℏ\hbar we can test whether a theory is uniformly asymptotic.

Figure S1 shows the ratio of the rate constant calculated using various approximate theories to the exact result at four different values of ℏ\hbar as a function of τ/τc\tau/\tau_{\rm c} for this model. The parameters considered in the top left panel, where ℏ=1\hbar=1, are equivalent to Fig. 5 of the main text and also to those considered in Ref. 3. In this regime the numerical deviation between the theory of Ref. 3 and the new theory presented here is relatively small. However, it is notable that approaching the crossover temperature from below kRef. 3k_{\text{Ref.~\cite[citenum]{\@@bibref{Number}{Upadhyayula2023UniformInstanton}{}{}}}} initially tracks the increase in the instanton rate, before oscillating to underestimate the rate just above the crossover temperature. This behaviour is exacerbated as ℏ\hbar decreases, with kRef. 3k_{\text{Ref.~\cite[citenum]{\@@bibref{Number}{Upadhyayula2023UniformInstanton}{}{}}}} following kinstk_{\text{inst}} more and more closely below the crossover temperature, and the oscillation becoming more and more pronounced. In contrast, the ratio between the exact result and the theory presented in this work approaches 1 as ℏ→0\hbar\to 0 for all values of τ/τc\tau/\tau_{\rm c} as is expected for a uniform theory.
